In summary, our research is concerned with
the following topics:
the study of the metallicity distribution of stars in nearby open clusters, with particular attention to the influence of stellar mass on chemical composition and on the presence of giant planets.
the study of the chemical abundances of open clusters and their relation with the formation of giant exoplanets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formation of giant exoplanets is favored by high metallicities in stars with masses larger than 1.2 Msun.
the mass-giant planet connection is not yet fully understood, and the metallicity-giant planet connection has not been confirmed.
the metallicity-giant planet correlation is not confirmed in the case of the open clusters studied here.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the metallicities derived for the giant stars are in good agreement with the metallicities of the dwarf stars in the same cluster.
the derived average metallicites of these open clusters are all close to solar, with a slight trend of increasing metallicity with increasing mass of the host star.
the metallicity of the clusters is not an important parameter for the formation of giant planetary companions, while stellar mass is.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metallicity and mass of the host star play a crucial role in the formation of giant exoplanets.
the metallicity of the host star is not a good predictor of the presence of giant planets.
the metallicities for giant and dwarf stars in open clusters are in good agreement.
